selected_passages.text: A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

selected_passages.title: sources/News_publisher_files_class_action_antitrust_suit_against_Google_citing_AI_s_harms_to_their_bottom_line
selected_passages.text: Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. The suit claims these practices violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act by discouraging users from visiting publisher websites, potentially causing publishers to lose 20-40% of their traffic, and seeks an injunction requiring consent for using publisher data to train AI models.

selected_passages.title: raw:sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair
selected_passages.text: For the US, which has to prove that Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, this legal case could be an uphill battle. But for the rest of us, it offers a rare opportunity for some insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share. Is it still focused on being the best? Or, as has been alleged, does it use its ubiquity to squeeze us for money even at the expense of product quality? How ‘organic’ are Google’s results? This month, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray, which alleged that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people’s search queries for maximum ad revenue. The example given was replacing a search for “children’s clothing” with “NIKOLAI-brand kidswear”. Loading Google rejected this in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards, but the degree to which it was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google’s part. A suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times.

selected_passages.title: sources/5_things_we_learned_so_far_about_the_Google_antitrust_case
selected_passages.text: Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified in a U.S. antitrust trial defending the company's $26.3 billion spending to secure default search engine status across platforms, including a major deal with Apple. selected_passages.title: raw:sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair
selected_passages.text: Grey herself is a former vice-president at DuckDuckGo, a privacy-focused company founded explicitly to counter giants such as Google. She admits that she may have misinterpreted the evidence, but maintains that Google manipulates Search to maximise ad revenue. So what does Google say? In a post on X, Google’s official search liaison, Danny Sullivan, said ad systems do not affect the organic results, i.e. the list of blue links in search results that are not sponsored. “Ad keyword matching is a long-standing and well-known process that is designed to connect people to relevant ads. A separate process, which has nothing to do with ads, is used to match organic results to a query,” he said. “It’s no secret that Google Search looks beyond the specific words in a query to better understand their meaning ... If you make a spelling mistake, or search for a term that’s not on a page but where the page has a close synonym, or if you aren’t even sure exactly how to search for something, our meaning matching systems help.” It is true that some search queries result in more ads than others, and what ads you get can vary wildly depending on your request, which is the result of the keyword matching Google uses to sell ads. But Google denies pushing users towards the most monetisable subjects.

selected_passages.title: sources/5_things_we_learned_so_far_about_the_Google_antitrust_case
selected_passages.text:
- Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine.
- Approximately $18 billion of the payment went directly to Apple.
- Google's deal with Apple has been in place since 2003.
- When users switch their browser homepage to Google, they perform 15% more searches.
- When users switch away from Google, their searches drop by 27%.
- Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella offered to spend $15 billion annually to make Bing the default on Apple devices.
- Google gets 16 times more data than Bing every day.
- The DOJ accused Google of systematically destroying chat messages via the history-off option.
- Pichai changed the history-off default for chat in February to comply with a litigation hold.
- The trial is expected to continue for several weeks.
- The case is compared to the 1990s U.S. trial against Microsoft.
- If ruled against Google, the outcome could resemble the Microsoft settlement.
- Google might be required to turn over collected data to other search engines.
- The FTC sued Amazon in September for anticompetitive strategies.
- The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over its third-party app policies.
- There is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook regarding Instagram and WhatsApp.
- Google's legal chief David Drummond sent an angry letter to Microsoft in 2005.
- The letter accused Microsoft's Internet Explorer default setting as anticompetitive.
- Google's internal chat logs were deleted despite being subject to a litigation hold.
- Pichai testified on October 28 regarding the search head's revelations.
- The DOJ filed a separate claim in January alongside eight states.

If you make a spelling mistake, or search for a term that’s not on a page but where the page has a close synonym, or if you aren’t even sure exactly how to search for something, our meaning matching systems help.” It is true that some search queries result in more ads than others, and what ads you get can vary wildly depending on your request, which is the result of the keyword matching Google uses to sell ads. But Google denies pushing users towards the most monetisable subjects.
